title: Two Big Stick Insect Species Emerge from Australia - Nautilus
gist: University of Sydney biologists, publishing in Austral Entomology, described two new stick insect (Phasmatodea) species and recovered one species in Australia. The species had gone unrecognized even though these insects are among Australia's most photographed and most reported. The article is a short teaser.

insights.claim: A University of Sydney study in Austral Entomology described two new stick insect species and recovered one previously described species in Australia.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shows that biodiversity baselines are still incomplete even in heavily surveyed regions, which matters for biodiversity-linked disclosure and offset markets.
insights.quote: the study announced two new species and one recovered species in Australia
insights.locator: Published in the journal Austral Entomology

insights.claim: Some of Australia's most photographed and most reported insects include species that science has never formally recognized, so large amounts of observation data do not guarantee correct taxonomy.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Big observational datasets, such as citizen-science photos, still need expert validation, which is a caution for data-driven nature-monitoring products.
insights.quote: we’re still finding species that have escaped scientific recognition
insights.locator: “Taxonomy is often a bit like detective work,”

insights.claim: Cryptic stick insect species can be told apart once enough people are looking at them, which points to wide participation as the route to taxonomic discovery.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A small data point for the value of crowdsourced observation platforms in biodiversity monitoring.
insights.quote: with enough people around, even cryptic walking stick insects eventually get recognized
